style: Read as a calm, intelligent documentary narrator, but brisk and urgent. Short sentences, clear pauses, no theatrics.

shorts.text:
Google helped train an AI to predict which hospital patients will die.

It beat the hospitals' own tools.

Here's what nobody checks. The records were called anonymous.

Dates. Notes. A hospital. Add what Google already knows about where you go, and one patient sued, saying anyone could be identified.

The case was dismissed. Not because that was impossible. Because he couldn't show harm.

So what was the AI really for?

Google helped train an AI to predict who will die.

You woke up. You picked up your phone. You searched something. Opened the map. Watched a video. Paused it. Went back. Stopped for two seconds on one image.

Nobody was watching. A machine was counting.

In a hospital, a pulse is a reading. On your phone, so is a pause.

Alone, nothing. Together, a prediction of what you'll do next.

And the more certain the prediction, the more expensive the ad.

You never saw the meter.

You pay nothing. So who pays?

The advertiser. And they're not buying your time. They're buying a probability.

The more certain it is that you'll click, the more it costs.

Alphabet made more than four hundred billion dollars last year. Most of it from ads.

The product was never the ad. The product is certainty.

You pay nothing. So who pays?

One thing to do this week.

Open your Google account settings. Find one thing it keeps about you. Just one.

You don't have to delete anything. You just have to see the meter.

Most people never have.

Open it. Look. That's the whole assignment.
